V6.1.2.note: No user-chosen passwords, so no list of words to keep out of them.

V6.1.3.note: All five pathways, their proof, account namespace, controls and strength, in one table.

V6.3.1.note: As documented: per-IP limits, 5 emails per address per 15 minutes, 10 wrong codes per address per 24 hours.

V6.3.2.note: No default accounts exist. The demo sign-in is refused in production whatever is configured.

V6.3.3.note: Every pathway is a single factor (an inbox, or an Apple or Google account). The rationale (the money data lives on the phone behind its own PIN lock; the server holds account, household and billing state) is documented; adding a second factor is a product decision.

V6.3.4.note: Every route is classified, and a new one fails the matrix until it is; every pathway is documented, with the same session at the end.

V6.4.1.note: Sign-in links (256 random bits) and codes (6 digits from a CSPRNG) expire after 10 minutes and work once; they never become a long-term credential.

V6.4.2.note: No password hints or security questions exist anywhere in the sign-in code.

V6.4.3.note: No passwords to reset: a lost session is replaced by a new sign-in link.

V6.4.4.note: No multi-factor authentication factors to lose.

V6.5.1.note: A sign-in link and a code each work once.

V6.5.2.note: No lookup secrets (backup codes) exist. (Sign-in link tokens are stored only as a hash.)

V6.5.3.note: Codes come from crypto.randomInt, link tokens from crypto.randomBytes(32).

V6.5.4.note: Codes are 6 random digits (about 20 bits), links 256 bits.

V6.6.1.note: No SMS or phone delivery of codes.

V6.6.2.note: A code is replaced by the next one requested, and on the phone a link works only for a request made there for the same email. Gap: an earlier LINK stays usable for the rest of its 10 minutes after a newer one is requested.

V6.6.3.note: Codes: 10 verifications per IP per minute and 10 wrong codes per address per 24 hours. Links carry 256 bits.

V6.8.1.note: Accounts are namespaced by provider (acct_apple_ and acct_google_ plus the provider's user id); a provider's email never selects an account.

V6.8.2.note: Apple and Google tokens are refused unsigned (alg none), with another algorithm, signed by another key, or tampered with.

V6.8.4.note: No function requires a stronger or more recent sign-in; the documented assumption is single-factor strength for every pathway.

V7.1.1.note: Inactivity (30 days) and the absence of an absolute lifetime are documented, the latter as an owner decision (V7.3.2).

V7.1.2.note: Documented: sessions per account are not capped; each device sign-in is its own session.

V7.1.3.note: Documented: a session started with Apple or Google is independent of the provider's own session.

V7.2.1.note: Every token is verified by the API (one guard for all protected routes); the app never decides for itself.

V7.2.2.note: Sessions are per-sign-in tokens (RS256 access JWTs, random refresh tokens), never static keys.

V7.2.3.note: Refresh tokens are 256 bits from crypto.randomBytes, stored only as a hash.

V7.2.4.note: Each sign-in issues a new session. Gap: signing in again does not end the device's previous session on the server; it lasts until its refresh token expires or is used.

V7.3.1.note: A session unused for 30 days ends: its refresh token is refused at 30 days and works the second before.

V7.3.2.note: No absolute lifetime: each refresh starts a new 30 days, so an app in use stays signed in. Documented; whether to cap it (signing users out periodically) is a product decision.

V7.4.1.note: Sign-out revokes the refresh token at once. Gap (F77): the access token works until it expires, at most 15 minutes; a per-account revocation time already exists for account deletion.

V7.4.2.note: Deleting an account ends every session, link and code of that account, then every access token issued before it.

V7.4.3.note: No authentication factor can be changed (no passwords, no MFA settings).

V7.4.4.note: The only authenticated surface is the app; sign-out is on its Profile screen.

V7.4.5.note: There are no administrators and no operator tool to end a user's sessions short of deleting the account.

V7.5.1.note: No account attribute used for sign-in can be changed: there is no email change, phone number or MFA setting.

V7.5.2.note: Users cannot list or end their other sessions.

V7.6.1.note: Documented: a Zeno session neither follows nor ends the Apple or Google session.

V7.6.2.note: A session starts only after the user chooses a pathway and confirms it (opens the link, enters the code, or approves with Apple or Google); the app also requires the age consent first.

V8.1.1.note: Function-level (public, own secret, signed in) and data-level rules (own data only; households for members) are documented.

V8.1.2.note: Field-level rule documented: a member changes only their own spend line; there are no other roles.

V8.2.1.note: Every route's access is pinned; a new route fails the matrix until it is classified.

V8.2.2.note: The account comes from the verified token, never a parameter; a stranger gets 403 on a household with identical bodies, an unknown id 404.

V8.2.3.note: A member's spend write lands on their own line whatever the body says; the member id comes from the token.

V8.3.1.note: Every decision is made in the API; the app holds no authority.

V8.4.1.note: Households are the only shared space; every household route checks membership first.

V9.1.1.note: Signatures are checked before claims are used, for our tokens and the providers'.

V9.1.2.note: RS256 only: alg none, HS256 and a missing key id are refused.

V9.1.3.note: Keys come only from our own configured key pair and from Apple's and Google's fixed JWKS URLs, chosen by kid; jku, x5u and jwk headers are never read.

V9.2.1.note: exp to the second, and nbf when present, for our tokens and the providers'.

V9.2.2.note: Access tokens need our issuer and audience, which provider ID tokens never carry; refresh tokens are opaque and only accepted by /auth/refresh.

V9.2.3.note: Our audience is checked on every access token; a provider token must carry our client id.

V9.2.4.note: Our signing key issues tokens for one audience only (zeno-mobile).

V10.1.1.note: Tokens live only in the app's keychain and travel only to our API (and Gmail's to Google); the website handles none.

V10.1.2.note: Each sign-in has its own random nonce; the provider gets its SHA-256, the API checks the token carries it (F10).

V10.2.1.note: Gmail connect uses the code flow with PKCE (a code_verifier, no client secret).

V10.2.2.note: Each provider's tokens are checked against that provider's own issuer, keys and audience: an Apple token is refused on the Google route and the reverse.

V10.3.1.note: The API accepts only access tokens with its audience.

V10.3.2.note: The account (sub) is the basis of every decision; no scope or delegation claims are issued.

V10.3.3.note: Users are identified by sub, an account id derived once and never reassigned, under our single issuer.

V10.3.4.note: No route requires a particular sign-in strength or recency.

V10.5.2.note: Users are identified by the provider's sub, namespaced by provider.

V10.5.3.note: No metadata discovery: issuers and JWKS URLs are fixed in the code.

V10.5.4.note: The ID token's audience must be our configured client id; a wrong or missing audience is refused.
